Demo.ts:badge: DEMO · the ideal path, no mistakes
Demo.ts:bar.captionsOnly: No narration in this language yet: captions only
Demo.ts:beat1.body: The Country's Ministry of Health emails a Statement of Interest to the GDHCN Secretariat. WHO checks that the Country is eligible and accepts the Terms of Participation, then invites it to onboard and sends the technical specifications.
Demo.ts:beat1.title: Ask to join
Demo.ts:beat2.body: The Country names four people: a Business Owner, a Legal representative, a Technical lead, and a Key Master, who runs the Country's keys. The Key Master creates a Signing CA, a TLS and an Upload certificate for testing, and a separate set for production. The Signing CA's private key goes into an offline vault and never leaves the Country.
Demo.ts:beat2.title: Name the team, make the keys
Demo.ts:beat3.body: Each authorised person creates a GPG key with their official email address. The Technical lead puts the public keys, never the private ones, in private GitHub repositories, and invites WHO's bots: tng-bot-dev for testing, and tng-bot for production. The Key Master signs the release tag from the terminal.
Demo.ts:beat3.title: Public keys to GitHub
Demo.ts:beat4.body: Before production, the Legal representative sends a Letter of Application for each trust domain the Country joins, or one Letter for joining with no trust domain yet. It names the four contacts, the GPG key fingerprints and the production repository. The certificates themselves stay in the repository for tng-bot to collect.
Demo.ts:beat4.title: Send the Letter of Application
Demo.ts:beat5.body: WHO confirms the named people face to face, or through the diplomatic channel, and checks that the email inside every GPG key matches the Letter.
Demo.ts:beat5.title: WHO verifies the people
Demo.ts:beat6.body: WHO Operations takes over. tng-bot clones the signed tag, verifies it against the onboarded GPG keys, and collects the public keys. Test keys are signed automatically and whitelisted.
Demo.ts:beat6.title: tng-bot collects the keys
Demo.ts:beat7.body: Production keys are verified by WHO, and signed with the WHO Trust Anchor in an air-gapped process. The Trust Anchor's private key never sits on the online gateway.
Demo.ts:beat7.title: WHO signs PROD offline
Demo.ts:beat8.body: The Technical lead connects to a test gateway with the TLS client certificate. Testing can run on DEV, UAT or PROD. The dry run uploads a Document Signer Certificate, revokes one, downloads the trust list and validates samples. When it passes, WHO opens production.
Demo.ts:beat8.title: Test before going live
Demo.ts:beat9.body: A Document Signer Certificate, signed by the Signing CA, is packaged, signed with the Upload certificate, uploaded to production and found in the trust list. One is revoked to prove that works, the results go by email, and a confirmation tells the Country and WHO that onboarding is complete. From here, renewing certificates on time is the Country's job.
Demo.ts:beat9.title: Go live
Demo.ts:cast.certsChip: Signing CA · TLS · Upload for UAT and for PROD
Demo.ts:cast.legal.duty: WHO's contact on legal and policy
Demo.ts:end.lede: That is the whole journey on the ideal path. In the game, your team makes each call, and wrong calls come back, sometimes much later.
Demo.ts:end.title: Back to the start

data.ts:icvp.how1: Nordavia joined the network once: it proved who it is and shared only its public keys, which the network added to a trust list.
data.ts:icvp.how2: Coralia keeps a copy of that trust list, so its officer checks the signature, that the key hasn't been revoked, and the vaccination rules, with no call to Nordavia or to the network. It works offline.
data.ts:icvp.how3: The QR code carries the certificate itself, with only what a border needs to know. Nobody can change it without breaking the signature.
data.ts:icvp.how4: The network never carries Mary's vaccination record and never sees her name.
data.ts:icvp.idea: The certificate carries its own proof. The network carries trust, not data.
data.ts:icvp.subtitle: A digital yellow fever certificate that any border can check
data.ts:icvp.summary: Mary lives in Nordavia and is travelling to Coralia, which asks for proof of yellow fever vaccination. At the travel clinic she is vaccinated and the nurse records it as usual. Behind the screen, Nordavia turns that record into a standard digital vaccination certificate (the International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis, ICVP), signs it with a key that never leaves the country, and gives Mary a QR code on her phone and on her paper yellow card. At the border in Coralia, the port health officer scans it and the check passes in seconds. A forged card, signed with a key no trusted country published, fails.
data.ts:icvp.title: Mary's Yellow Card
data.ts:icvp.why: Vaccination certificates for travel are one of the first uses of the network, and the same signed code works whether it is shown on a phone or printed on the paper yellow card.
data.ts:maternal.how1: Nordavia's signature on the code is checked against the public keys the network publishes, so Coralia knows the reference is genuine.
data.ts:maternal.how2: The summary stays at home, held by Nordavia under its own rules, and is fetched directly from Nordavia only for an authorised health worker, with consent.
data.ts:maternal.how3: The network never carries Amina's health information and never sees her name.
data.ts:maternal.how4: Her baby's birth and first vaccines are recorded in Coralia in a record of his own, and Nordavia's clinic carries on his schedule with no gaps and no repeated doses.
data.ts:maternal.idea: The QR code points to the record; it is not the record. The network carries trust, not data.
data.ts:maternal.subtitle: A mother's care record that can safely cross a border
data.ts:maternal.summary: Amina is seven months pregnant in Nordavia and plans to give birth near her mother, across the border in Coralia. Her antenatal care, including a penicillin allergy, stays in Nordavia as a standard International Patient Summary. What she carries is a signed QR code that points to that summary and holds no medical details. When labour comes early at a hospital she has never seen, the midwife scans the code with Amina's consent, checks the signature against Nordavia's public key, confirms her identity, and only then fetches the summary from Nordavia. The allergy is right there.
data.ts:maternal.title: Amina's Journey
data.ts:maternal.why: Continuity of care across borders matters most in the first 1,000 days of a child's life, and the International Patient Summary already supports it at summary level.

glossary:anchor.def: WHO's top-level key that signs every country's PROD keys. It is kept offline, never on the Gateway.
glossary:dev.def: Development environment. Optional, for early technical trials.
glossary:dsc.def: Signs the health documents, such as vaccination certificates, that verifiers check.
glossary:gateway.def: WHO's server where participants exchange public keys and trust lists.
glossary:github.def: GitHub is a website for storing code and files in repositories, with a full history of every change. In GDHCN onboarding, each country keeps its public keys and certificates in its own private GitHub repositories, and WHO's tng-bot collects them from there.
glossary:gpg.def: A personal key pair each named person uses to sign. WHO checks the email inside it against the Letter of Application.
glossary:prod.def: Production: the live Trust Network Gateway. Real keys, signed offline by WHO.
glossary:repo.def: A folder on GitHub with version history. Private means only the people and bots you invite can see it.
glossary:sca.def: Your country's own trust anchor. Its private key signs your Document Signer Certificates and is kept offline.
glossary:tls.def: Proves your backend's identity when it connects to the Gateway (mutual TLS).
glossary:tngbot.def: WHO's automated GitHub account. tng-bot-dev serves DEV and UAT; tng-bot serves PROD. It only reads repositories it is invited to.
glossary:top.def: The five commitments, TOP0 to TOP4, that every GDHCN participant accepts: from following the technical specifications to meeting legal and policy standards.
glossary:uat.def: User Acceptance Testing: the test gateway where you prove everything works before production. Test keys only.
glossary:upload.def: Signs the packages of certificates your country uploads to the Gateway.

scenario:renew.brief: {country} is live. Its certificates expire: recommended validity is about 4 years for the SCA, 2 for a DSC, and 1 to 2 for Upload and TLS. WHO's certificate expiry dashboard (one each for DEV, UAT and PROD) shows {country}'s Upload certificate has 21 days left.
scenario:renew.choices.us.text: We do. We track expiry ourselves, renew in good time (for example a month before expiry) and send WHO the new certificate
scenario:renew.choices.who.consequence.w: {country}'s Upload and TLS certificates expired. Uploads stopped and the backend lost its connection.

The dashboard shows expiry dates, but no one sends reminders: each participant tracks its own certificates. Upload and TLS certificates must be renewed in good time, for example a month before expiry, and the new ones sent to WHO.
scenario:renew.choices.who.text: WHO will send a reminder before anything expires
scenario:renew.docs.0.title: Certificate expiry · PROD · {code}
scenario:renew.learn: Renewing certificates on time is {country}'s job for as long as it stays in the network.
scenario:renew.prompt: Who makes sure they are renewed in time?
scenario:renew.success.note: New Upload certificate made and sent to WHO. Renewal dates are in the team calendar.
scenario:renew.title: Stay live
scenario:repos.brief: {technicalFirst} creates the [[repo|private GitHub repositories]] that [[tngbot|WHO's bot]] will read.
scenario:repos.choices.onebot.consequenc: tng-bot serves PROD. tng-bot-dev serves DEV and UAT.
scenario:repos.choices.public.consequenc: The repositories have to be private.
Private repositories hide the uploader's identity.
scenario:repos.choices.public.text: Make them public so WHO can find them easily
scenario:repos.choices.right.text: A private repo per environment; invite tng-bot-dev to UAT and tng-bot to PROD
scenario:repos.docs.0.title: Repository setup

scenario:sca.brief: The SCA's private key is the root of trust for every Document Signer Certificate {country} will ever issue.
scenario:sca.choices.repo.consequence.wh: A private key left the country. It has to be treated as compromised: revoke it, regenerate, and prepare the key material again.
Only public keys go to GitHub. Private keys never cross the {country} boundary.
scenario:sca.choices.repo.text: In the GitHub repo next to the public keys, so nothing gets lost
An online server can be compromised. If the SCA key leaks, every certificate it vouches for is in doubt.
Keep the SCA offline, with more than one person needed to use it. A hardware security module or smart card adds further protection.
scenario:sca.choices.server.text: On the backend server, so signing is quick
scenario:sca.choices.vault.text: Offline, in the vault, under multi-person control
scenario:sca.docs.0.lines.1: Whoever holds it can speak for {country}
scenario:sca.docs.0.title: SCA private key
scenario:sca.learn: Private keys stay inside {country}, and the SCA key stays offline.
scenario:sca.success.note: SCA private key locked in the offline vault.
scenario:sca.title: Protect the trust anchor
scenario:soi.brief: {country} wants to issue digital health certificates that other countries can verify. The first move is a formal Statement of Interest to WHO.
scenario:soi.choices.gateway.consequence: The Gateway refused the connection. {country} has no certificates registered, and the Gateway only accepts signed key material over mTLS.
Paperwork travels by email to the Secretariat. The Gateway carries keys, never letters.
scenario:soi.choices.gateway.text: Upload it to the Trust Network Gateway
No one at WHO watches a repository it hasn't been told about. tng-bot only reads repositories it is invited to, much later in onboarding.
The Statement of Interest goes to gdhcn-secretariat@who.int.
scenario:soi.choices.github.text: Put it in a GitHub repository for WHO to find
scenario:soi.docs.0.lines.2: {country} wishes to join the Global Digital Health Certification Network as a Participant.

scenario:tag.brief: WHO's bot takes the latest git tag and checks its signature against your onboarded GPG keys. {keymasterFirst} marks the version WHO should use.
scenario:tag.choices.none.consequence.wh: tng-bot clones the latest tag. With no tag, there is nothing to take over.
Tag each version you want WHO to use, and sign it.
scenario:tag.choices.none.text: Skip the tag; the bot will take the latest commit
scenario:tag.choices.terminal.text: Sign it from the terminal with git tag -s, using {keymasterFirst}'s GPG key
scenario:tag.choices.web.text: Create it on the GitHub website; it's quicker
scenario:tag.docs.0.lines.0: GitHub website: Releases → Create a new tag

scenario:tag.learn: Sign the git tag locally, from the terminal or an IDE. Tags made on the GitHub website can't be verified by tng-bot.

scenario:team.brief: WHO needs named people it can verify. {business}, the Business Owner, puts the team together.
scenario:team.choices.four.text: Name all four, each with an official government email address
The Letter of Application must name the people authorised to provide {country}'s key material, with their contact details. It can't go out with a blank.
WHO verifies the named people in person or through the diplomatic channel, so they have to be named up front.
scenario:team.choices.later.text: Let the software vendor handle the keys and name the people later

ui.ts:about.p1: A learning tool that turns the WHO SMART Trust onboarding process into choices a country team makes. Step numbers refer to the published process at smart.who.int/trust, which remains the authority. The GDHCN Administrative and Operational Framework is authoritative for definitions.
ui.ts:about.p2: Simplifications: steps are grouped into moments, some checks are shown at a convenient point in the story, and game days are illustrative.
